questions.stem: A Python list `a` holds 1,000,000 numbers. Which of these operations takes the longest?
questions.explanation: Inserting at index 0 shifts all 1,000,000 items one place to the right: O(n). Reading or writing by index, even in the middle or with a negative index, is a single address calculation, O(1), and `append` is O(1) amortised.

questions.stem: Why can an array read `a[i]` in O(1) time, whatever the value of i?
options: It computes the address as start + i × slot size, without searching
It starts at a[0] and steps forward i times very quickly
It keeps a sorted copy of the items and uses binary search
Arrays are small enough to be scanned in a single step
questions.explanation: The slots are equal-sized and contiguous, so the position of item i is one calculation. Stepping forward i times would cost O(i): that is what a linked list has to do, not an array.

questions.stem: An array holds 8 items at indices 0 to 7 and has room for more. How many of the existing items must move to insert a new item at index 2?
questions.explanation: The items at indices 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 each move one slot right to open a gap: 6 items. In general, inserting at index i into n items moves n − i of them. 2 counts the items *before* the gap, which stay where they are.

questions.stem: What do `a.pop()` and `a.pop(0)` cost on a Python list of n items?
questions.explanation: Removing the last item leaves no gap, so nothing moves. Removing the first item leaves a gap at index 0, so every remaining item shifts one place left: O(n). Both look like a single call, but they do very different amounts of work.

questions.stem: A dynamic array starts empty with capacity 1 and doubles its capacity whenever an append finds it full. What is its capacity after 9 appends?
questions.explanation: The capacity goes 1 → 2 (at the 2nd append) → 4 (3rd) → 8 (5th) → 16 (9th). After 8 appends all 8 slots are full, so the 9th append triggers a resize to 16. Capacity is not the same as length: the array now holds 9 items in 16 slots.

questions.stem: A dynamic array starts empty with capacity 1 and doubles whenever an append finds it full. During 16 appends, how many element copies do the resizes make in total?
questions.explanation: Resizes happen at the 2nd, 3rd, 5th and 9th appends and copy 1, 2, 4 and 8 items: 15 copies, fewer than 2n. Spread over 16 appends that is about one copy each, which is why append is O(1) amortised. 120 = 0 + 1 + … + 15 is what growing by just one slot at a time would cost.

questions.stem: Which statement about `append` on a Python list is correct?
options: Every append is O(1), even when the list has to grow
Every append is O(n), because the list is copied each time
Most appends are O(1); an occasional one copies everything, so the average is O(1)
Append is O(log n), because the capacity doubles
questions.explanation: When the list is full, that one append copies every item into a bigger block, so a single append can be O(n). Because the capacity grows by a constant factor, such copies are rare and n appends cost O(n) in total: O(1) per append on average (amortised). Claiming *every* append is O(1) ignores the resize.

questions.stem: A 3 × 4 grid (3 rows, 4 columns) is stored row by row in one flat array. At which flat index is `grid[2][1]`?
questions.explanation: Row-major index = row × columns + column = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9: rows 0 and 1 fill indices 0 to 7, so row 2 starts at 8. Multiplying by the number of rows instead of columns gives 2 × 3 + 1 = 7; swapping row and column gives 1 × 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.stem:
What does this print?

```python
grid = [[0] * 3] * 2
grid[0][0] = 5
print(grid)
```
questions.explanation: `* 2` copies the *reference* to the inner list, not the list itself, so both rows are the same list object and the change appears in both. Build the rows separately, `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]`, to get `[[5, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]`.

questions.stem:
How many swaps does `reverse` make on a list of 7 items?

```python
def reverse(a):
    i, j = 0, len(a) - 1
    while i < j:
        a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
        i += 1
        j -= 1
```
questions.explanation: It swaps positions (0, 6), (1, 5) and (2, 4); then i = j = 3, so the loop stops and the middle item stays put. In general it makes ⌊n/2⌋ swaps: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. 4 would mean swapping the middle item with itself, which `i < j` prevents.

questions.stem: In an unsorted array of n items, what does it cost to read the item at a known index, and to find the index of a known value?
options: Reading by index is O(n); finding a value is O(1)
Reading by index is O(1); finding a value is O(n)
questions.explanation: Reading by index is one address calculation. Finding a value in an unsorted array means checking the items one by one until it turns up: n checks in the worst case. Fast indexing does not help, because you do not know which index to compute.

questions.stem:
What is `a` after this code, and how many of the existing items had to shift?

```python
a = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23]
a.insert(2, 42)
```
questions.explanation: `insert(2, 42)` puts 42 at index 2, the third slot, so 15, 16 and 23 each move one slot right. It inserts rather than overwrites (overwriting would be `a[2] = 42`, which shifts nothing and loses 15).
Every one of the r × c cells is visited once. O(r + c) would be visiting one row and one column only. For a square n × n grid this is O(n²), yet it is still linear in the number of cells.

options: None, because the pointers meet first
questions.explanation: Sums: 1 + 11 = 12 (too big, j moves left), 1 + 8 = 9 (too small, i moves right), 3 + 8 = 11 (too big), 3 + 6 = 9 (too small), 4 + 6 = 10: found on the 5th sum. 15 is the number of pairs the brute-force method would try (6 × 5 / 2).

questions.stem: A dynamic array starts empty with capacity 4 and doubles when an append finds it full. How many resizes happen during 20 appends, and what is the final capacity?
questions.explanation: Appends 1 to 4 fill the first block. The 5th append resizes to 8, the 9th to 16 and the 17th to 32; appends 18 to 20 fit. "2 resizes, 16" forgets that 20 items do not fit in 16 slots, and "16 resizes, 20" is what growing by one slot at a time would do.

Each `x in a` scans the list and each `a.remove(x)` scans and shifts it: O(n) per line. If most items equal x, the loop runs up to n times, so the total is O(n²). It looks like one loop, but each line inside it is a hidden loop. Building a new list in one pass, `[v for v in a if v != x]`, takes O(n).
